interactive_questions.title: Dose-Response Simulation
interactive_questions.prompt: Adjust the dosage to find the THERAPEUTIC WINDOW (50-80% effect without toxicity).
interactive_questions.question: Set the dosage to achieve a therapeutic effect without toxicity.
interactive_questions.answer: A dosage that results in an effect between 50% and 80%.
interactive_questions.explanation: You found the safe zone! The goal is to maximize benefit while minimizing harm.

theory.title: The Therapeutic Window
theory.content:
The Therapeutic Window is the range of drug doses that treats disease effectively without causing toxic side effects.

Analogy Visual: The Salt in the Soup

  • Sub-therapeutic: Dose is too low to work.
  • Toxic: Dose is too high and damages the body.
  • Therapeutic Index (TI): A measure of drug safety. A wide TI means the drug is safe (e.g., Penicillin). A narrow TI means the safe dose is very close to the toxic dose (e.g., Warfarin).
theory.analogy: Cooking with salt. Too little, and the food is bland (ineffective). Too much, and it's ruined (toxic). The 'Therapeutic Window' is that perfect pinch that makes it taste good.
theory.application: Drugs with narrow therapeutic windows require 'Therapeutic Drug Monitoring' (TDM). We regularly check blood levels of drugs like Lithium or Digoxin to ensure the patient isn't accidentally poisoned.

interactive_questions.title: The Journey of a Drug
interactive_questions.prompt: Place the four main stages of pharmacokinetics (ADME) in the correct chronological order.
interactive_questions.question: Arrange the ADME steps in order.

theory.title: ADME: Pharmacokinetics
theory.content:
Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to the drug.

Analogy Visual: Package Delivery

  1. Absorption: Entering the bloodstream.
  2. Distribution: Spreading to tissues/organs.
  3. Metabolism: Biotransformation (usually in the Liver) to make the drug water-soluble.
  4. Excretion: Removal from the body (usually via Kidneys/Urine).
theory.analogy: A package delivery: 1. Loaded onto the truck (Absorption). 2. Driven to your neighborhood (Distribution). 3. Unboxed and used (Metabolism/Action). 4. The box is recycled (Excretion).
theory.application: Liver failure slows Metabolism, causing drugs to build up to toxic levels. Kidney failure stops Excretion. In these patients, we must drastically lower drug doses to prevent overdose.

interactive_questions.title: Synergy and Antagonism
interactive_questions.prompt: Observe how combining drugs can alter their effects.
interactive_questions.question: Administering two drugs together results in a much stronger response than either drug alone. This is:
interactive_questions.explanation: Synergism occurs when drugs work together to produce an effect greater than the sum of their individual effects.

theory.title: Drug Interactions
theory.content:
Synergism (1+1 > 2): Two drugs amplify each other. Useful for pain relief (Opioid + Tylenol) or fighting infection (Antibiotic combos).

Analogy Visual: Synergy vs. Antagonism

Antagonism (1+1 < 2): One drug blocks another. Used in antidotes.
theory.analogy: Synergy is like two people lifting a heavy sofa together—they can lift far more than just the sum of what each could lift alone. Antagonism is like one person trying to open a door while another holds it shut.
theory.application: We use Antagonism to save lives. Naloxone (Narcan) is an antagonist that kicks opioids off brain receptors, instantly reversing a fatal overdose.
